note: Quotations are checked against the stored NASA documents at every build. The short answers and the sentences marked as readings are this project's own; they are not NASA conclusions and not operational advice.
source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.myth: A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off.
items.question: Kill the fans?
items.answer: On the space station, cutting the airflow starved the flame NASA tested, within two seconds. NASA's own guide still lists the belief as a misconception, its documents name the cases where it can fail, and on the Moon gravity keeps air moving after every fan has stopped.

groups.title: It held when the forced flow was the flame's only source of oxygen

items.quote: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s
items.says: A BASS-II test on the space station
items.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA TM, NTRS 20210011385

items.text: BASS-II in PSI: 129 test rows, with oxygen at the start between 13.6% and 22.2%. The table records conditions and gas readings. It has no column saying whether each flame went out.

groups.title: The fuel can bring its own oxygen

items.quote: the canister ignited, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke
items.says: Mir, 24 February 1997
items.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

items.quote: The flame finally extinguished itself
items.says: After three extinguishers
items.source: NASA History: 25 Years Ago, Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

items.text: The page calls the device a solid-fuel oxygen generator. That it fed its own flame, so that stopping ventilation could not have starved it, is our reading and not a sentence on the page.

groups.title: The visible flame is not the whole reaction

items.quote: This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction
items.says: Fuel droplets on the station
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: In PSI: the Cool Flames Investigation lists 87 droplet tests (PSI-39); the gas-burner follow-up marks 7 of its 179 normal-flame rows 'yes' under 'Cool flame?' (PSI-159).
Cool flames were seen on large droplets of particular fuels and on gas burners. Nothing here says cabin materials behave this way.

items.quote: the characteristic gas velocity of the minimum in the curve is on the order of 10 cm/s and also corresponds to a maximum in the flame spread rate
items.says: The flow at which solids burn most readily
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.text: Simple scaling puts the buoyant flow near a small flame in lunar gravity at about 6 to 11 cm/s: inside the range the guide calls most flammable. A bound from a formula, not a measurement.

items.quote: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.quote: the burn lasts for over two and a half minutes
items.says: Fabric and an acrylic rod burning in simulated lunar gravity on a spinning rocket
items.source: Ferkul et al., Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket, NTRS 20250010653 (abstract)

items.quote: the crucial mechanism of buoyant oxygen entrainment at the flame base is still present, but at a slower rate
items.says: NASA in 2026, on a marginal material on the Moon
items.source: Ferkul, Kralik and Liao, Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, extended abstract, NTRS 20260000646

items.text: NASA's LUCI flight, in simulated lunar gravity: the flame base on the fabric moved at 0.9 mm/s, against 1.5 mm/s in the same test on Earth. Slower, and it burned longer. Read from NASA's slides; the data are not in PSI.
Of 2,009 test rows in the 24 combustion records of PSI, 0 were taken in lunar or Martian gravity. 19 records are flight experiments in free fall and 5 are ground work.

items.quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity
items.says: 2025; the data are not in PSI
items.source: Ferkul et al., Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket, NTRS 20250010653 (abstract)

items.quote: Conduct the first-ever observations and measurements of flame spread on the Moon
items.says: An objective of the FM2 experiment
items.source: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

items.myth: A steady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment.
items.question: Can a fire burn steadily in still air, with no gravity to feed it?
items.answer: Yes. NASA's experiments burned candles, flame balls and fuel droplets for minutes in still microgravity gas.

items.myth: Because the reduced-gravity environment is inherently safer, terrestrial fire standards and tests represent a very conservative approach to fire safety.
items.question: Are tests on Earth a safe upper bound for space?
items.answer: Not always. NASA reports materials that burn at lower oxygen in microgravity and in Martian gravity than in the standard test on Earth.

groups.title: Materials that burned in less oxygen than on Earth

items.quote: is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth
items.says: The guide, on results from BASS and the standard upward-burning test
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.quote: the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen

items.source: Olson and Ferkul, Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test, NTRS 20130010991

items.quote: If proven for more materials, this may indicate the need to include a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits
